title: Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth
text:
In 2000 the finance professors Brad Barber and Terrance Odean, at the University of California, published a study of how ordinary people fared when they picked and traded stocks themselves. They obtained records from a large American discount brokerage covering more than 66,000 households from 1991 to 1996.

Over that period, the stock market as a whole returned roughly 17.9 percent a year. The average household earned about 16.4 percent after trading costs. That was respectable, but it trailed the market. The real difference showed up when Barber and Odean sorted households by how much they traded. The fifth of households that traded most turned over their portfolios more than twice a year, and they earned only about 11.4 percent a year after costs, far behind both the market and the households that traded least.

The stocks these active traders bought did not perform better than the ones they sold, at least not enough to cover the commissions and price spreads they paid for each trade. Their activity simply cost them money.

Barber and Odean argued that the most likely explanation was overconfidence: investors believed their information and judgment were better than they were, so they traded too often. In a follow-up study titled "Boys Will Be Boys," they found that men traded considerably more than women, and that the extra trading lowered men's returns more.
lesson: Activity is not the same as progress. If your decisions carry a cost each time you change course, make sure your confidence in each change is earned before you act on it.
location: University of California, Davis, USA (data from a US discount brokerage)
source: Barber, B. M., and Odean, T. (2000). Trading is hazardous to your wealth: The common stock investment performance of individual investors. Journal of Finance, 55(2), 773-806.
